Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON (CNN) -- Iran offered to stop attacking coalition troops in Iraq nearly four years ago in an attempt to get the West to accept Tehran's nuclear program, a British diplomat told the BBC in an interview aired Saturday. John Sawers, British ambassador to the U.N., told BBC of Iran approaching Western nations with offer. "The Iranians wanted to be able to strike a deal whereby they stopped killing our forces in Iraq in return for them being allowed to carry on with their nuclear program -- 'We stop killing you in Iraq, stop undermining the political process there, you allow us to carry on with our nuclear program without let or hindrance," said John Sawers, now the British ambassador to the United Nations, in the documentary, "Iran and the West: Nuclear Confrontation." The United States and other Western nations believe Iran is pursuing a nuclear weapons program, but Iran says it is developing nuclear capability to produce energy. Iran also has been accused of sponsoring terrorists and supplying weapons to Iraqi insurgents. The latter prompted a warning from the United States that such behavior by Tehran "would be regarded by us as enemy action," Philip Zelikow, a State Department counselor, told the BBC. Then, Iran began shopping its offer around Europe, Sawers said. Sawers, Britain's political director at the time, reveals the behind-the-scene talks from 2005 -- when roadside bombing against British and American soldiers in Iraq peaked -- were held with British, French and German diplomats at hotels in London, Paris and Berlin. "And then we'd compare notes among the three of us," Sawers told the BBC. The British government dismissed the offer and Iran's nuclear enrichment program restarted once again, the BBC reports . Iran has denied offering any such deal and reiterated its position Saturday. "Iran's high officials have repeatedly stated that Iran has not had any part in attacks against American and British forces, and there is no evidence to support these baseless accusations," Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Hassan Qashqavi said, according to the semi-official Mehr News Agency. Interviews with top brass from former President Bush's administration and British envoys indicate that Iran and the West had neared agreements several times in the past few years, but never reached success. Nick Burns, who was in charge of the Bush administration's State Department policy with Iran, said taking a tough approach with Iran didn't seem effective. "We had advocated regime change," Burns told the BBC. "We had a very threatening posture towards Iran for a number of years. It didn't produce any movement whatsoever." The documentary aired a day after the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security released a report stating that Iranian scientists have reached "nuclear weapons breakout capability." The report analyzed the finding of the U.N.'s nuclear watchdog agency, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA). However, an IAEA official who asked not to be named cautioned against drawing such dramatic conclusions from the data, saying Iran's stock of low-enriched uranium would have to be turned into highly enriched uranium (HEU) in order to be weapons-grade material. That hasn't been done, the official said. Meanwhile, Iran's relationship with the West continues to be strained, though both sides have indicated interest in holding direct talks. President Obama, in his first prime-time news conference held earlier this month, said the United States is looking for opportunities for "face-to-face" talks with Iran after an absence of diplomatic ties for nearly three decades. "There's been a lot of mistrust built up over the years, so it's not going to happen overnight," he said. And Iran's powerful parliament speaker and former nuclear negotiator, Ali Larijani, has called the Obama administration "an exceptional opportunity for Americans."

outputs.L1:
LONDON (CNN) — Iran offered nearly four years ago to stop attacking coalition troops in Iraq in an effort to persuade the West to accept Tehran’s nuclear program, a British diplomat said in a BBC interview broadcast Saturday.

John Sawers, now the British ambassador to the United Nations, told the BBC that Iran had approached Western nations with an offer.

“The Iranians wanted to be able to strike a deal whereby they stopped killing our forces in Iraq in return for them being allowed to carry on with their nuclear program — ‘We stop killing you in Iraq, stop undermining the political process there, you allow us to carry on with our nuclear program without let or hindrance,’” Sawers said in the documentary “Iran and the West: Nuclear Confrontation.”

The United States and other Western nations believe Iran is pursuing a nuclear weapons program, while Iran maintains that it is developing nuclear capabilities to produce energy.

Iran has also been accused of sponsoring terrorists and supplying weapons to Iraqi insurgents. The latter allegation prompted a warning from the United States that such conduct by Tehran “would be regarded by us as enemy action,” Philip Zelikow, a State Department counselor, told the BBC.

Iran then began presenting its offer across Europe, Sawers said.

Sawers, who was Britain’s political director at the time, revealed that the behind-the-scenes talks in 2005 — when roadside bombings targeting British and American soldiers in Iraq peaked — were held with British, French and German diplomats at hotels in London, Paris and Berlin.

“And then we’d compare notes among the three of us,” Sawers told the BBC.

The British government rejected the offer, and Iran’s nuclear enrichment program subsequently resumed, the BBC reported.

Iran has denied making any such offer and reiterated its position Saturday.

“Iran’s high officials have repeatedly stated that Iran has not had any part in attacks against American and British forces, and there is no evidence to support these baseless accusations,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Hassan Qashqavi said, according to the semi-official Mehr News Agency.

Interviews with senior officials from former President Bush’s administration and British envoys indicate that Iran and the West came close to reaching agreements several times in recent years but were ultimately unsuccessful.

Nick Burns, who oversaw the Bush administration State Department’s policy toward Iran, said a tough approach did not appear to be effective.

“We had advocated regime change,” Burns told the BBC. “We had a very threatening posture towards Iran for a number of years. It didn’t produce any movement whatsoever.”

The documentary aired one day after the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security released a report stating that Iranian scientists had achieved “nuclear weapons breakout capability.”

The report analyzed the findings of the United Nations’ nuclear watchdog agency, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).

However, an IAEA official who asked not to be identified cautioned against drawing such dramatic conclusions from the data, saying Iran’s stockpile of low-enriched uranium would have to be converted into highly enriched uranium (HEU) to become weapons-grade material. That has not been done, the official said.

Meanwhile, Iran’s relationship with the West remains strained, although both sides have expressed interest in holding direct talks.

President Obama, during his first prime-time news conference earlier this month, said the United States was seeking opportunities for “face-to-face” talks with Iran after nearly three decades without diplomatic relations.

“There’s been a lot of mistrust built up over the years, so it’s not going to happen overnight,” he said.

Ali Larijani, Iran’s powerful parliament speaker and a former nuclear negotiator, has called the Obama administration “an exceptional opportunity for Americans.”

**LONDON (CNN) —** A senior British diplomat said Iran proposed nearly four years earlier that it would halt attacks on coalition forces in Iraq if Western governments accepted Tehran’s continued nuclear activities.

John Sawers, Britain’s ambassador to the United Nations, told the BBC that Iranian officials approached Western countries about such an arrangement. Speaking in the documentary *Iran and the West: Nuclear Confrontation*, Sawers described the proposal as an exchange: Iran would stop killing coalition troops and interfering with Iraq’s political process, while the West would allow its nuclear program to continue without obstruction.

The United States and other Western governments suspect Iran of seeking nuclear weapons. Tehran insists, however, that its nuclear development is intended to generate energy. Iran has also faced allegations that it supports terrorist groups and provides arms to insurgents in Iraq.

Those accusations led Washington to warn that such conduct would be treated as hostile action. Philip Zelikow, then a State Department counselor, told the BBC that Iranian involvement of that kind “would be regarded by us as enemy action.”

According to Sawers, Iran subsequently presented its proposal to European governments. Sawers, who was Britain’s political director at the time, said secret discussions took place in 2005, when roadside-bomb attacks against British and American troops in Iraq were at their highest. British, French and German diplomats met in hotels in London, Paris and Berlin, then shared and compared their accounts of the talks.

The BBC reported that the British government rejected the proposal, after which Iran resumed its uranium-enrichment program.

Iran denied ever making such an offer and repeated that denial Saturday. Foreign Ministry spokesman Hassan Qashqavi said senior Iranian officials had consistently maintained that the country played no role in attacks on American or British forces. He added that there was no evidence for what he called unfounded allegations, according to the semi-official Mehr News Agency.

Interviews with senior officials from former President George W. Bush’s administration and with British diplomats suggested that Iran and Western countries came close to agreements several times in recent years but ultimately failed to finalize any of them.

Nick Burns, who oversaw Iran policy at the State Department during the Bush administration, said a confrontational strategy did not appear to work. He told the BBC that Washington had supported regime change and maintained a threatening stance toward Iran for years, yet this produced no progress.

The documentary was broadcast one day after the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security issued a report concluding that Iranian scientists had achieved a “nuclear weapons breakout capability.” Its assessment was based on findings by the United Nations’ nuclear-monitoring body, the International Atomic Energy Agency.

An unnamed IAEA official, however, warned against interpreting the information so dramatically. The official said Iran’s low-enriched uranium stockpile would first need to be converted into highly enriched uranium before it could qualify as weapons-grade material, and that this conversion had not occurred.

Relations between Iran and Western countries remained tense, although both sides expressed interest in direct negotiations. At his first prime-time news conference earlier that month, President Barack Obama said the United States was seeking opportunities for face-to-face discussions with Iran after almost 30 years without diplomatic relations. He cautioned that decades of mistrust could not be overcome immediately.

Ali Larijani, Iran’s influential parliamentary speaker and a former nuclear negotiator, likewise described the Obama administration as “an exceptional opportunity for Americans.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about British diplomat John Sawers claiming that Iran offered to stop attacks on coalition forces in Iraq in exchange for Western acceptance of its nuclear program.
counterfactuals.output:
# British diplomat says Iran linked Iraq attacks to nuclear concessions

**LONDON (CNN) —** Iran offered to halt attacks on coalition forces in Iraq if Western governments accepted Tehran’s nuclear program, according to senior British diplomat John Sawers.

Sawers said the proposal emerged during negotiations between Iran and European powers over Tehran’s nuclear activities. At the time, Western governments suspected Iran of supporting armed groups responsible for attacks on U.S. and British troops in neighboring Iraq.

According to Sawers, Iranian officials indicated that violence against coalition forces could be stopped in return for Western acceptance of Iran’s right to continue its nuclear work.

The claim suggests Tehran viewed its influence in Iraq and the nuclear dispute as connected elements of a broader negotiation with the West. Iran has long denied directing attacks on coalition troops, though U.S. and British officials have repeatedly accused it of supplying weapons, training and funding to Shiite militias.

Iran has also maintained that its nuclear program is intended solely for peaceful purposes, including civilian energy production. Western governments have argued that some of its activities could provide the capacity to develop nuclear weapons.

Sawers, who later served as chief of Britain’s foreign intelligence service, MI6, was closely involved in European diplomacy with Iran. Britain, France and Germany led early efforts to persuade Tehran to limit uranium enrichment in exchange for political and economic incentives.

His account highlights the complexity of those negotiations, which unfolded as coalition forces faced a growing insurgency in Iraq and as concerns mounted over Iran’s regional influence.

It was not immediately clear whether the alleged offer was formally presented or how Western officials responded. Iranian authorities have not publicly confirmed Sawers’ account.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the BBC documentary “Iran and the West: Nuclear Confrontation,” including Iran’s alleged 2005 proposal, Western concerns about its nuclear ambitions, and reactions from Iranian officials.
counterfactuals.output:
The BBC documentary **“Iran and the West: Nuclear Confrontation,”** part of the 2009 series *Iran and the West*, traces the escalating dispute over Iran’s nuclear program from the early 2000s through the Ahmadinejad presidency.

- **Iran’s alleged 2005 proposal:** Former Iranian negotiators say Tehran offered a compromise under which it would continue only limited uranium enrichment—reportedly a pilot-scale program of roughly 3,000 centrifuges—while accepting extensive international inspections and other safeguards. Iran also floated foreign participation in its enrichment facilities as a way to demonstrate that nuclear material would not be diverted. The documentary suggests the proposal was rejected because Britain, France, Germany and especially the United States insisted that Iran suspend enrichment altogether.

- **Western concerns:** Western governments feared that mastery of enrichment would give Iran the ability to produce highly enriched uranium for a bomb, even if Tehran initially operated under safeguards. Iran’s concealment of parts of its program, questions from the International Atomic Energy Agency, missile development and hostile rhetoric—particularly under President Mahmoud Ahmadinejad—deepened suspicions. Western officials therefore saw even a limited enrichment capability as a possible step toward a nuclear-weapons “breakout” option.

- **Iranian reactions:** Iranian officials interviewed in the film insist that the program was peaceful and that uranium enrichment was Iran’s legal right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Figures including former negotiators argue that Tehran had offered meaningful concessions but received little in return. They portray the Western refusal as evidence that the real objective was to deny Iran nuclear technology altogether, and say the rejection weakened moderates, strengthened hardliners and contributed to the later confrontation.

Overall, the documentary presents the crisis as a product not only of nuclear technology but also of accumulated mistrust, missed diplomatic opportunities and incompatible demands: Iran sought recognition of a limited right to enrich, while Western governments wanted suspension before broader negotiations could proceed.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed news report on behind-the-scenes negotiations between Iran, Britain, France, Germany, and the United States over Iraq and Iran’s nuclear enrichment program.
counterfactuals.output:
**Western powers tested parallel diplomatic tracks with Iran over Iraq and nuclear enrichment**

*This report reconstructs the diplomacy of 2005–06 from official statements, diplomatic briefings and contemporaneous reporting. Because the negotiations were largely private, some accounts differed over the sequencing and substance of proposals.*

**VIENNA/WASHINGTON —** Behind public warnings over Iran’s nuclear ambitions, Britain, France, Germany and the United States pursued a complicated, sometimes divided diplomatic effort aimed at testing whether Tehran could be engaged on two separate crises: the deteriorating security situation in Iraq and Iran’s refusal to suspend uranium enrichment.

The discussions unfolded on nominally distinct tracks. European governments led direct nuclear negotiations with Tehran, while Washington—then lacking formal diplomatic relations with Iran—considered limited contacts focused on Iraq. In practice, the two issues repeatedly overlapped. Iranian officials sought recognition of their country’s regional influence and nuclear rights, while Western governments debated whether concessions in one area might encourage cooperation in the other—or allow Tehran to use Iraq as leverage in the nuclear dispute.

### A narrow opening over Iraq

The Iraq channel emerged as sectarian violence intensified and coalition forces faced attacks from militias that U.S. and British officials said received support, weapons or training from networks linked to Iran. Tehran denied directing the violence and argued that instability resulted from the U.S.-led invasion and occupation.

American and Iranian officials signaled a willingness in early 2006 to hold talks limited to Iraq. The proposed discussions were expected to involve the U.S. ambassador in Baghdad and an Iranian counterpart rather than senior officials from the two governments. Washington insisted the agenda would not include the nuclear program or broader normalization of relations.

Iran presented the opening differently. Senior Iranian figures portrayed the talks as an opportunity to discuss the withdrawal of foreign forces and the transfer of greater authority to Iraq’s elected government. Tehran also maintained close ties with leading Shiite political parties and militias, giving it substantial influence in Baghdad.

Britain, whose forces were concentrated in southern Iraq, supported efforts to reduce Iranian assistance to armed groups but remained cautious about a negotiation that could legitimize Tehran’s regional role without producing verifiable changes. France and Germany were less directly involved in the Iraq channel but watched closely for signs that Washington might strike a bilateral understanding affecting the nuclear talks.

The contacts did not initially develop into a sustained negotiating process. Each side questioned the other’s intentions, and escalating violence in Iraq narrowed the political space for engagement. U.S. officials feared Iran wanted to use talks to divide the coalition or demonstrate that Washington needed Tehran’s help. Iranian officials suspected the United States was offering only a tactical conversation while continuing to seek Tehran’s isolation.

### Europe’s nuclear initiative stalls

The more formal diplomatic effort centered on Iran’s nuclear program. Britain, France and Germany—the “EU-3”—had negotiated with Tehran since 2003, seeking a suspension of activities that could eventually provide Iran with material for a nuclear weapon.

Iran insisted that its program was peaceful and that uranium enrichment for civilian purposes was a right guaranteed under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. Western governments countered that years of concealed nuclear work, unresolved questions from international inspectors and research potentially relevant to weaponization made unrestricted enrichment unacceptable.

Under earlier agreements with the Europeans, Iran had temporarily suspended enrichment-related activity while the parties negotiated a long-term settlement. Tehran later complained that Europe’s proposals offered vague economic benefits but no reliable security assurances, access to advanced technology or recognition of an industrial enrichment program.

The talks deteriorated after Iran resumed uranium-conversion work at Isfahan and later enrichment-related activity at Natanz. The International Atomic Energy Agency’s governing board subsequently reported the issue to the United Nations Security Council.

Behind closed doors, European negotiators debated how far to go in acknowledging Iran’s claimed nuclear rights. One possible formula would have recognized Iran’s general treaty rights while requiring it to suspend enrichment for an extended period and restore broader international monitoring. Another centered on Russian enrichment of uranium for Iranian reactors, keeping the most sensitive part of the fuel cycle outside Iran.

Tehran signaled interest in cooperation with Russia but rejected any arrangement that permanently barred enrichment on Iranian territory. Iranian officials argued that reliance on foreign suppliers would leave the country vulnerable to political pressure.

### Washington considers incentives

The Europeans repeatedly told Washington that diplomacy would be more credible if the United States joined the offer rather than remaining outside the negotiations while threatening sanctions. Iran viewed American hostility—not simply the technical nuclear dispute—as central to the crisis.

Inside the U.S. administration, officials argued over whether direct involvement would strengthen the diplomatic coalition or reward Iranian defiance. Skeptics said Tehran was using negotiations to gain time, improve its technical capabilities and divide Europe from the United States. Supporters of engagement argued that Washington could not demand far-reaching concessions without stating what Iran would receive in return.

The resulting compromise was a coordinated package prepared by the United States, Britain, France, Germany, Russia and China. It combined possible economic and technological incentives with the threat of escalating penalties if Iran refused to suspend enrichment. Measures under discussion included assistance with civilian nuclear energy, guarantees of reactor fuel, support for trade and investment, and possible easing of restrictions affecting Iranian access to aircraft parts and other technology.

The United States also moved toward conditional participation in direct nuclear negotiations, provided Iran first suspended enrichment-related activities. That condition was intended to prevent talks from continuing while Iran expanded its program. Tehran objected that suspension should be the outcome of negotiations, not the price of admission.

Security guarantees remained the most politically sensitive question. Iranian officials wanted assurance that the United States would not seek regime change or attack Iran. Washington was unwilling to give an unconditional guarantee, particularly while accusing Tehran of supporting militant groups and destabilizing Iraq.

### European unity masks tactical differences

Britain generally favored close alignment with Washington and a firm timetable for Iranian compliance. France also backed the suspension demand but periodically explored formulas that might preserve limited Iranian nuclear activity under strict supervision. Germany, with significant commercial ties to Iran and no permanent seat on the Security Council, emphasized incentives and the need to avoid military escalation.

The three European governments nevertheless concluded that public disunity would weaken their position. Their common strategy was to offer Tehran a choice between cooperation—with economic, technological and political benefits—and increasing isolation through the Security Council.

Diplomats said one objective was to prevent Iran from portraying the dispute as a confrontation solely with Washington. Russian and Chinese participation was therefore crucial. Both countries opposed an Iranian nuclear weapon but were more reluctant than the Western powers to impose sanctions or endorse coercive measures.

### Tehran sought to keep the tracks separate—when useful

Iranian officials alternated between separating and linking the Iraq and nuclear issues. They rejected American attempts to raise the nuclear program in an Iraq-only dialogue, arguing that each dispute required its own framework. At other moments, Tehran highlighted its ability to influence stability across the region, implicitly reminding Western governments that pressure on the nuclear file could carry wider costs.

Western officials likewise denied making an explicit bargain under which Iranian help in Iraq would be exchanged for flexibility on enrichment. Privately, however, they recognized that progress—or confrontation—on one track would shape the political atmosphere surrounding the other.

No evidence emerged of a formal agreement linking militia activity in Iraq to nuclear concessions. The negotiations instead resembled parallel tests of intent: Washington wanted proof that Iran would restrain allied groups and comply with nuclear demands; Tehran wanted proof that engagement would produce recognition, security and relief from economic pressure.

### The core dispute remained unresolved

The talks exposed a fundamental gap that technical proposals could not bridge. Western governments sought a suspension before substantive negotiations, seeing it as a safeguard against Iran using diplomacy to perfect enrichment. Iran regarded the same demand as an attempt to force surrender before talks began.

The Iraq channel was constrained by equally profound mistrust. Washington viewed Iranian influence largely through the lens of armed groups and attacks on coalition personnel. Tehran saw itself as an indispensable neighbor whose interests could not be excluded from the future of Iraq.

The diplomacy delayed immediate escalation and produced a more coordinated international position, but it failed to resolve either dispute. Iran continued advancing its nuclear capabilities, while Iraq remained an arena of competition as well as occasional indirect contact between Tehran and Washington.

The episode established a pattern that would recur in later negotiations: European governments acting as intermediaries, the United States debating whether and how to engage directly, Iran demanding recognition of its nuclear rights and regional standing, and all sides insisting that diplomacy was preferable while preparing for the possibility that it would fail.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain the reported Iranian offer to halt support for attacks against Western troops in Iraq, why Britain rejected it, and how it relates to subsequent nuclear diplomacy under Presidents Bush and Obama.
counterfactuals.output:
During the Iraq war, Iranian intermediaries reportedly told British officials that Tehran could restrain—or end support for—Shiite militias attacking British and other coalition forces if London adopted a more accommodating position in the dispute over Iran’s nuclear program. Accounts differ over the date, channel, and precise terms, and Iran denied directing the attacks, so it is best understood as a reported exploratory proposal rather than a formal, documented agreement.

Britain rejected the linkage for several reasons:

- It appeared to amount to bargaining with the safety of British troops: Iran would stop conduct Britain regarded as unlawful only in return for nuclear concessions.
- Accepting it might reward the use of proxy violence and encourage further coercion.
- British officials doubted that Tehran could be trusted to deliver—or that reduced attacks could be verified.
- London did not want to break from the common U.S.–European position that Iran first had to suspend uranium enrichment and comply with international nuclear demands.

The episode nevertheless foreshadowed a broader policy question: whether the nuclear file should be negotiated separately from Iran’s regional behavior.

Under President George W. Bush, Washington initially resisted direct bargaining with Iran unless it first suspended enrichment. That position softened late in his administration: the United States joined multilateral diplomacy more directly, including sending Undersecretary of State William Burns to a 2008 meeting with Iranian representatives. No comprehensive bargain resulted.

President Barack Obama went further. His administration opened direct and secret channels, eventually producing the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action. The JCPOA was deliberately limited to nuclear restrictions, monitoring, and sanctions relief; it did not require Iran to end support for militias or change its policies in Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, or elsewhere.

Thus, the later diplomacy was not an acceptance of the alleged “stop attacks in exchange for nuclear concessions” offer. Rather, it reflected a related but distinct judgment: a verifiable nuclear agreement could be pursued on its own merits even while the United States and Britain continued to oppose Iran’s regional and proxy activities. Critics saw this as overlooking coercive behavior; supporters saw compartmentalization as the only practical way to prevent an Iranian nuclear weapon.

counterfactuals.output:
## Iran’s Nuclear Standoff Exposes the Limits of Diplomacy—and the Risks of Its Failure

**LONDON/WASHINGTON/TEHRAN —** Iran’s nuclear program remains at the center of its troubled relationship with the West, combining a technical dispute over uranium enrichment with a wider struggle involving sanctions, regional influence and decades of mutual distrust.

The 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, or JCPOA, temporarily eased the confrontation by limiting Iran’s nuclear activities in exchange for sanctions relief. But the United States’ withdrawal from the agreement in 2018 and Iran’s subsequent expansion of its nuclear program have left diplomacy weakened and the risk of escalation considerably higher.

Sir John Sawers, the former head of Britain’s Secret Intelligence Service, has argued that any durable approach must recognize both the dangers of Iran’s nuclear advances and the need for sustained engagement. His public comments have emphasized that intelligence and sanctions may slow proliferation, but cannot by themselves resolve the political conflict. From that perspective, negotiated restrictions backed by intrusive inspections remain more credible than attempts to isolate Tehran indefinitely.

Philip Zelikow, a former counselor at the U.S. State Department, has placed the issue in a broader strategic context. He has warned that nuclear negotiations cannot be separated entirely from Iran’s regional activities or from the security calculations of Israel and the Arab states. A narrowly technical agreement may buy time, his analysis suggests, but it will remain vulnerable unless governments address the political order surrounding it.

Nicholas Burns, a veteran American diplomat and former undersecretary of state for political affairs, has similarly supported diplomacy while stressing the importance of allied unity. Burns has argued that Washington is most effective when it coordinates closely with Britain, France, Germany and other partners, preserves economic pressure, and leaves open a credible negotiating channel. Military action, he has cautioned, could delay Iran’s program but would be unlikely to eliminate the knowledge and infrastructure behind it.

That logic also shaped Barack Obama’s defense of the JCPOA during his presidency. Obama said the agreement cut off Iran’s principal routes to a nuclear weapon by limiting enrichment, reducing stockpiles and expanding international monitoring. He acknowledged that the accord did not resolve disputes over Iran’s missile program, support for regional armed groups or hostility toward Israel. His central argument was more limited: preventing a nuclear-armed Iran was urgent enough to justify an enforceable agreement focused specifically on the nuclear issue.

Iranian officials have presented the dispute very differently. Ali Larijani, a former parliamentary speaker and nuclear negotiator, has repeatedly defended Iran’s right under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty to pursue peaceful nuclear technology, including enrichment. He has also accused Western governments of demanding restrictions while failing to deliver dependable sanctions relief. For Tehran, Larijani’s comments reflect a longstanding contention that compromise brings little benefit if Western economic pressure can be restored or expanded despite Iranian compliance.

The competing narratives expose the central obstacle to renewed diplomacy. Western governments fear that Iran’s growing enrichment capacity could allow it to move rapidly toward weapons-grade material, even if Tehran has not made a final decision to build a bomb. Iranian leaders, meanwhile, see sanctions, covert operations and military threats as evidence that the West seeks strategic capitulation rather than verifiable nuclear limits.

Verification therefore remains essential but insufficient. International Atomic Energy Agency inspections can provide information about declared facilities and nuclear material, yet inspectors cannot create political trust. Nor can technical formulas alone settle disputes over sanctions relief, guarantees of compliance or Iran’s role across the Middle East.

The positions associated with Sawers, Zelikow, Burns, Obama and Larijani differ sharply, but they converge on one point: the nuclear dispute is inseparable from the collapse of confidence between Iran and the West. A renewed agreement would require more than limits on centrifuges and uranium. It would need a credible enforcement mechanism, meaningful economic incentives and sustained coordination among the major powers.

Without such an arrangement, Iran could continue moving closer to nuclear-threshold status while Western governments rely increasingly on sanctions, sabotage and deterrence. That path may postpone a final reckoning, but it also raises the possibility that miscalculation—not deliberate strategy—will determine what comes next.
